title: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating as country grapples with turmoil and higher yields
description: A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration as part of a nationwide mobilization over rising living costs, fuel prices and education fundin
body: A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration as part of a nationwide mobilization over rising living costs, fuel prices and education funding in Paris, France, on Oct. 17, 2026.Ibrahim Ezzat | Anadolu | Getty ImagesMoody's opted to maintain its credit rating on France as the country contended with a week of civil unrest and rising political risk.The agency kept France's credit rating at Aa3, a level Moody's still deems "high grade," but it also maintained its negative outlook on the nation."The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report. Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow the deficit. Investors were anticipating Moody's rating decision as France, the second-largest economy in the euro zone, grappled with protests and a sharp surge in bond yields. "This political instability, also visible in the current social tensions, risks hampering the French government's ability to address key policy challenges such as an elevated fiscal deficit, rising debt burden, and durable increase in borrowing costs, thus leading to a more rapid weakening in the sovereign's key credit metrics than we currently expect," Moody's said in its report Friday.This week, the nation's 10-year bond yield surpassed 5% for the first time since 2002. The spread against German bunds is also at a 15-year peak. Currently, France's deficit-to-GDP ratio is at roughly 5.5% of its GDP, sharply above the 3% limit for member nations in the European Union. The country faces more than $1 trillion of debt that will mature by 2030. Just a month ago, the French finance ministry warned that the nation's debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to hit 121.7% in 2027.At the same time, France has been rocked by protests. Last weekend, more than 500,000 people marched to express their frustration against declining public services and high costs of living.

schema.headline: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating as country grapples with turmoil and higher yields

title: College campuses have (largely) gone silent. Can practicing small talk and phone-free spaces change that?
description: Charlie Harker had high hopes for college.Before starting her freshman year in 2023, the Lebanon, Ohio, resident had planned to meet people through cl
body: Charlie Harker had high hopes for college.Before starting her freshman year in 2023, the Lebanon, Ohio, resident had planned to meet people through clubs or at the dorms. She'd expected there would be an open, vibrant atmosphere ripe for making friends. She'd quickly find her people."And then I got to school," says the 21-year-old senior at the University of Cincinnati. "I didn't know anyone on my floor. No one had their door open. No one would really talk to you." That fun and peer-filled campus life she'd been promised by both family and pop culture turned out to be, at least to some extent, a relic of the past.Harker's college experience is fairly common these days. From 2003 to 2025, 20-to 24-year-olds' socializing and communicating in the U.S dropped 52%, from an average of 64 minutes per day in their leisure time to an average of just over 30 minutes per day. Over the same period, 15-to 19-year-olds' leisure time socializing dropped 32% to 38 minutes, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Students these days view school as more "transactional" than in the past, says Steven Rogelberg, Chancellor's professor of organizational science, management and psychology at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. "You go there, you take your classes, and then you leave." That's a problem for a variety of reasons. If they're not meeting in class or stopping each other in the hallways, young people may be missing out on developing both friendships and social skills, which are critical for long-term life and career success. Making small talk, for instance, can help forge both personal and professional relationships down the line, says Kristie Patten, dean of NYU's Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development.Also essential: building confidence, which can come both from successfully navigating social situations and making painful mistakes. Without that practice, both campus and life can become more insular and sterile."Parents and school systems, and maybe even legislators, are going to have to deal with this if we want a future where we have kids and adults who understand how to be social with one another," says Lance Garrison, dean of the College of Professional Psychology at The Chicago School."The trajectory we are on right now is one toward increasing isolation, increasing loneliness, increasing anxiety." Some students and schools are tackling their campus antisocial problems head-on. CNBC Make It spoke with 15 students, educators and mental health experts to see how we got here — and where we might be going. 'I think a lot of people just got used to not hanging out'Today's college students were already at a disadvantage, socially speaking, well before stepping foot on campus. Not only were they forced to isolate during middle school or high school because of the pandemic, many are also finding fewer spaces to meet in real life, as malls and movie theaters — traditional meeting grounds for young people — have shuttered in recent years. "A lot of them never had to build those muscles of how do you socialize in person," says Chicago-based therapist Andrew Fishman.Charlie Harker.Courtesy Charlie HarkerFor some teenagers, that inability to connect meant new norms. "I think a lot of people just got used to not hanging out with people after school," says Harker about high school. For others, it's made approaching people that much scarier. The less you have a chance to talk to someone new, says Garrison, "the more anxious you are going to be about engaging in those types of activities."On campus, that could also mean high rates of loneliness. When asked how often they feel or felt lonely in college in a CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll conducted in August 2026, a quarter of 18-to 34-year-olds said "always" or "often," versus just 14% of 35-to 64-year-olds. The modeled error estimate for this survey was plus or minus 3.0 percentage points.The dining hall is 'people with AirPods and watching YouTube sitting alone'When they finally reach the hallowed halls of their universities, many students are constantly connected to a device. Often, they are heads down in screens or engrossed in whatever's happening in their headphones.Before class, 19-year-old Karla Berrueto, a junior in standing at the University of Houston, reports: "No one really talks to each other." Twenty-one-year-old Jean Antoine, a senior at Loyola Marymount University, offers a similar appraisal. At the dining hall, it's "more of people with AirPods and watching YouTube sitting alone" than talking, he says.Even when people go out of their way to connect offline, they're frequently stymied. Franco Geldart, a 20-year-old sophomore at Northeastern University, joined a cooking club his freshman year. He found striking up conversations with people a bit awkward. Often, "I was sitting [there] for an hour and I didn't speak with a single person," he says.Most of the students CNBC Make It spoke with attended up to a handful of parties per year. Some described them as events you attend with friends and leave, rather than fluid opportunities to engage with new people. The trajectory we are on right now is one toward increasing isolation, increasing loneliness, increasing anxiety.Lance GarrisonDean, College of Professional Psychology at the Chicago SchoolAsked how often they initiate or initiated conversations with people at school they didn't know, 31% of Gen Z said "rarely" or "never," according to the CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll, versus 26% of Millennials and 22% of Gen X.Another new element of today's campus is the plethora of online platforms on which one can be called out for doing … anything, really, making even the most mundane decisions terrifying.Yik Yak and Fizz are anonymous digital message boards. Fizz alone is live at more than 800 U.S. college campuses, according to its website. Many schools also have dedicated Barstool Sports Instagram pages, often affiliated with the popular sports blog but unaffiliated with the schools. All three may contain posts making fun of individual students' behavior.Harker remembers going to a football game her freshman year and losing the friend she came with. She felt paralyzed, scared of trying to befriend people who'd reject her and even more terrified of getting photographed sitting at the game by herself. "If I just sat there alone," she says she thought, "would I get on the Barstool page?" What would the social repercussions of that be?Yik Yak, Fizz and Barstool Sports did not respond to CNBC Make It's request for comment.'We're going to bring back house parties'To be clear, young people are still forging connections on campus. They are figuring it out. Some are even experiencing similar levels of social fluidity as prior generations.And some see what's been happening on campus and taking action. Geldart is working on an application for a new club at Northeastern this year called Wildcard. It would partner with existing clubs and do one-off drop-ins in which members from each club would be randomly paired up for a project."It's just to get people talking," he says.At New York University, students have spearheaded a campus-wide initiative called NYU IRL, centered on connecting in the age of technology. With the help of a coalition of deans, faculty, staff and grad students, NYU IRL projects include phone-free spaces, a phone breakup challenge with Catherine Price, author of "How to Break Up With Your Phone," and a video series about how to make small talk. More than 1,000 students have signed up for the phone breakup challenge alone.For her part, Harker found someone she knew at the football game where she'd lost her friend and the two became each other's go-to game date. She joined a sorority and now lives in a house with a number of her friends.Harker's working on creating more opportunities for people to meet. She remembers attending one house party her freshman year, for example. "It was the best experience I ever had," she says. It was an easy, casual way to get to know people. Harker and her roommates are now trying to replicate that experience."We have this thing," she says, "we're going to bring back house parties."

schema.headline: College campuses have (largely) gone silent. Can practicing small talk and phone-free spaces change that?

title: Investors are starting to find opportunities in the battered bond market
description: A trader works at the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 19, 2026. NYSEEven after another bond market rout Friday, investors are turning their attention
body: A trader works at the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 19, 2026. NYSEEven after another bond market rout Friday, investors are turning their attention toward Treasurys,  anticipating that yields may be topping out.The benchmark 10-year note spent the day flirting with the psychologically important 5% level as oil prices surged and a fresh consumer survey showed that inflation expectations remain a good distance above the Federal Reserve's 2% goal.Still, some market participants see reason for hope in a market bludgeoned this year over worries about rising prices, tensions in the Middle East and stiff competition from artificial intelligence hyperscalers flooding the market with debt.Bank of America's Michael Hartnett in a client note declared "The Price is Right" on the battered Treasury market, which he noted has seen its worst long-run return in the past 100 years.The investment strategist noted in his weekly money-flow summary that the "secular contrarian [trade] would be adding bonds," drawing a parallel to similar long-run negative returns for stocks and commodities that later proved to be good entry pointsDespite the negative returns and soaring yields this year, investors are putting money into fixed income and government debt in particular. Treasurys saw $5.4 billion in inflows over the past week, part of $12.1 billion overall into the bond market, according to data compiled by BofA. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, a $47.3 billion fund that offers exposure to long-dated government debt, has seen $1.14 billion in fresh investor cash over the past month.One reason for investor enthusiasm is the simple belief that the Treasury sell-off has exhausted itself, with the market pricing in the various risks to the market and now at least ready to stabilize.Thursday's trading saw the 10-year yield crater a massive 19 basis points, or 0.19 percentage point. Stock Chart IconStock chart icon10-year yield this weekNicholas Colas, co-founder of DataTrek Research, calculated the gain as a "3 standard deviation move," or well outside the expected trading range for the flagship Treasury security for the day. Given current conditions, including another sanguine reading on unemployment claims Thursday, Colas wrote in his daily market note that the trade "catalyst was not a sudden change in the market's view on the U.S. economy.""Our read is that the Treasury market is taking the equity and corporate debt market's collective angst about AI-related CapEx funding as a sign incremental issuance will slow," he added. "With less of this paper coming to market, Treasuries face less competition for capital."Historically, stocks and bonds generally move opposite each other. As risk appetite grows, investors generally eschew the safety of bonds, and vice versa.That hasn't been the trend lately, as Friday's slide in the stock market coincided with an aggressive sell-off in bonds, a trade largely driven by fears of escalating oil prices hitting both asset classes.However, Colas said history suggests the correlation again will return, making a stocks/bonds mix still "a reasonable approach, recent painful history notwithstanding."Moreover, he called the Thursday plunge in yields "an important signal.""The fever of higher rates may not have entirely broken," he said, "but [Thursday] was a solid step in the right direction."

schema.headline: Investors are starting to find opportunities in the battered bond market

title: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI'
description: Stephen Squeri, chairman and chief executive officer of American Express Co., speaks during an Economic Club of New York event in New York, US, on Thu
body: Stephen Squeri, chairman and chief executive officer of American Express Co., speaks during an Economic Club of New York event in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 10, 2022.Stephanie Keith | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAmerican Express is cutting thousands of employees as the leading credit card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more of its internal processes.Amex is eliminating 5% of its global workforce and taking a $336 million restructuring charge, CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts Friday on the company's third-quarter earnings call. The firm had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025. Chief Financial Officer Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI.""You don't want to automate processes that are not optimally structured," Le Caillec said. "So what we're doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years."The Amex announcement reflects a broader trend across financial services, where banks are working to replace repetitive roles with AI automation. On Thursday, Barclays confirmed plans to trim 5,000 jobs — also roughly 5% of its staff — in another tech-driven cost initiative. The moves come even as the sector is enjoying robust profits from growing consumer spending and resilient credit.During the analyst call, Squeri said the charge was to improve the company's efficiency."We've got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become [a] more agile and efficient organization," Squeri said.'Run rogue'Squeri devoted a 10-minute section of his prepared remarks to his views on AI, focusing mainly on how it will be used to personalize experiences and offers for Amex cardholders.While the CEO emphasized the need to meet customers' desires to use AI, including agents, he added that Amex is "not going to let assistants run rogue through our system.""We need to protect our customers [and] merchants, and we're only going to allow agents to access our systems that are either approved through API or MCP channels," he said, citing two ways to securely connect outside platforms with Amex systems.Amex posted quarterly results that topped Wall Street profit expectations. Adjusted earnings per share were $4.68, beating the $4.48 average estimate of analysts, according to LSEG.The company raised its full-year earnings guidance to a range of $18.30 to $18.60 per share, on an unadjusted basis, up from its previous target of $17.30 to $17.90.That metric was helped by proceeds from Amex's sale of its stake in Global Business Travel Group, part of which went into the restructuring plan, Le Caillec said. Total revenue rose 9% to $20.06 billion, coming in slightly below Wall Street's $20.12 billion LSEG forecast. Executives attributed part of the spending drag to recent exits from small business co-brand partnerships.Shares of the card company fell roughly 4% in afternoon trading.

schema.headline: American Express is cutting 5% of its workforce to 'prepare for AI'

title: TikTok U.S. hunts for multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources tell CNBC
description: TikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC, amid a global scramble for digital infrastructu
body: TikTok's U.S. entity is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources told CNBC, amid a global scramble for digital infrastructure deals. The company, officially TikTok USDS Joint Venture, operates the social media platform in the U.S. and has sounded out opportunities to obtain capacity over the coming years, two people familiar with the discussions, who asked to remain anonymous as they weren't authorized to share the information, told CNBC.TikTok U.S. is looking for four gigawatts of compute power by the early 2030s, one source said.Companies across the world are looking to secure more compute capacity as artificial intelligence workloads become more prominent. A company spokesperson told CNBC that the company "runs primarily on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in the U.S. and Oracle will continue to be our primary cloud infrastructure provider."Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, or OCI, typically runs in facilities that Oracle leases. CNBC has approached Oracle for comment.There are signs TikTok U.S.' product plans could require extra compute going forward. The company has numerous machine learning roles live on its website. A job advert posted by TikTok states that the company is "shipping a flagship B2B AI product at the frontier of large-model inference and creative automation."TikTok U.S. localizes algorithm trainingTikTok USDS Joint Venture was established in 2026 in compliance with U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order mandating the divestiture of TikTok in the U.S. from its Chinese parent company, ByteDance. In January, TikTok U.S. said it would "retrain, test, and update" its prized recommendation algorithm, which is built on machine learning, on U.S. user data. The company's recommendation algorithm will be "secured in Oracle's U.S. cloud environment," it said.TikTok U.S. has three managing investors, Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX, each holding 15%. The Dell Family Office, the investment firm of Michael Dell, is also an investor. ByteDance retained 19.9% of the new entity.

schema.headline: TikTok U.S. hunts for multiple gigawatts of computing capacity, sources tell CNBC

title: Restaurant earnings will test whether owning more brands pays off
description: A sign is posted in front of a Chili's restaurant in Rohnert Park, California, on Dec. 13, 2024.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesRestaurant stocks have s
body: A sign is posted in front of a Chili's restaurant in Rohnert Park, California, on Dec. 13, 2024.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesRestaurant stocks have split sharply this year. And it could be tied to how many brands they own.Shares of Brinker International, Darden Restaurants and Restaurant Brands International are up roughly 32%, 18% and 12%, respectively, year to date. Those companies all own more than one restaurant chain, with brands collectively ranging from Chili's to Olive Garden, LongHorn Steakhouse, Burger King and Tim Hortons.Meanwhile, stocks like McDonald's, Chipotle, Cava, Wendy's, Shake Shack and Domino's have all dropped this year, with several down double-digit percentages. Those companies all have one core chain to their names.Those share moves underscore what some analysts see as the benefits of a diversified restaurant business, especially at a time when any misstep can make cash-strapped consumers go elsewhere when they dine out. Investors will get another look at how operating multiple chains — or not — is affecting performance when major restaurant companies report quarterly results starting next week. One company that could be watching is Inspire Brands, the owner of chains like Dunkin', Buffalo Wild Wings and Jimmy John's, which is moving toward going public. A business built around one main restaurant concept depends more heavily on that brand holding consumers' attention, whereas a company with a portfolio has other potential sources of sales if one brand loses momentum.That cushion can be critical, but only if another chain is strong enough to pick up the slack, according to some Wall Street analysts."Darden is probably the best case of the scale and size and diversity of business," said Nick Setyan, a restaurant analyst at Mizuho Securities. "If one business isn't doing well, the other ones are." Igor Golovniov | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesSetyan said that dynamic has played out between Darden's key brands — Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse — over recent quarters. LongHorn's growth has outpaced Olive Garden's for months, and in the latest reported quarter, LongHorn's comparable sales rose 6.2% compared with Olive Garden's 1.1%.KeyBanc Capital Markets also cited the range of Darden's portfolio as a positive in an October research note, saying it gives the company "exposure to a broad range of consumers." The company's fine dining and casual offerings can be beneficial in a K-shaped economy where consumer spending can vary by income.The firm has a buy-equivalent rating on Darden and a $237 price target, compared with a price of around $215 as of Thursday.Restaurant Brands International, similarly, offers exposure to different categories and markets through Burger King, Tim Hortons and Popeyes. But its portfolio does not fully insulate the company from a weak brand. Tim Hortons owner to purchase Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen. The parent company of Tim Hortons and Burger King said it will pay US$1.8 billion cash to buy the Popeyes chain.Randy Risling | Toronto Star | Getty ImagesIn the second quarter, Burger King's U.S. comparable sales accelerated to 8.5%, from 5.8% in the first quarter, while Tim Hortons' Canadian comparable sales slowed to just 0.1%, from 1.5% over the same period. That left Burger King's turnaround carrying more of the portfolio as Tim Hortons stalled.Setyan said Burger King's recent strong performance has been central to the company's momentum, helped by its ability to better communicate its value items to customers as McDonald's sales growth slowed."If it weren't for Burger King's current performance, I don't know if [Restaurant Brands] would be going so well," he said.Mizuho initiated coverage of Restaurant Brands on Oct. 20 with a buy-equivalent rating and an $85 price target. Shares traded at about $76 as of Thursday.A focus on one brand can also be a strength. Starbucks and Cheesecake Factory have been restaurant-stock standouts this year, showing how a clear brand identity and investment can drive outperformance when execution and customer demand click. Their shares have climbed 21% and nearly 123%, respectively, this year.And Starbucks, for its part, said it would not buy Chipotle after reportedly considering a massive buyout that would have diversified its business.

schema.headline: Restaurant earnings will test whether owning more brands pays off

title: Two ex-FBI officials charged with allegedly lying about Hunter Biden probe: DOJ
description: Las Vegas Review-Journal | Tribune News Service | Getty ImagesTwo former senior FBI officials were taken into custody on Friday after being charged wi
body: Las Vegas Review-Journal | Tribune News Service | Getty ImagesTwo former senior FBI officials were taken into custody on Friday after being charged with lying to Congress about their roles in investigations into Hunter Biden, top Department of Justice officials announced.The former officials, 46-year-old Nikki Floris and 56-year-old Bradley Benavides, surrendered on arrest warrants Friday morning, the DOJ said in a press release.The charges were filed less than two weeks before the midterm election, breaking with longstanding DOJ guidance discouraging actions that could affect upcoming political races.The announcement also comes amid growing concerns that President Donald Trump — who refused to accept his 2020 election loss and tried repeatedly to overturn those results — is looking for ways to challenge potential Republican midterm losses. On Thursday, the DOJ filed an unusual lawsuit against Alaska seeking to preemptively challenge the results of that state's Senate race if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses.The charges unveiled Friday morning accuse the two ex-FBI agents of lying in 2023 testimony before the House Judiciary Committee about their agency's probe of Hunter Biden, the now-56-year-old son of former President Joe Biden.The agents were "actively involved" in federal investigations of Hunter Biden, which began in 2019 on tax- and money-laundering-related matters, but said otherwise in separate interviews before the House panel, according to an FBI special agent's affidavit in support of the charges."Floris and Benavides allegedly lied to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations, with one claiming they only learned about it from Wikipedia — despite evidence showing their involvement in helping shape the public narrative about Hunter Biden's laptop right before the election," U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in an X post.FBI Director Kash Patel said on X that the charges "stem from an ongoing investigation into the since-dissolved FBI Foreign Influence Task Force."Floris and Benavides, who both worked on that task force, testified that it "was not involved in the Hunter Biden investigations," Patel wrote. "Documentary evidence, contemporaneous communications, and witness accounts contradict their testimony."Attorneys for Floris called the charges "nonsense," and accused the Trump administration of deliberately filing them just before the Nov. 3 midterm election in hopes of gaining political advantage."Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts," read a statement from her counsel, including Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle Freeny. "It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they wrote."The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points," their statement added. "It's another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki's day in court."

schema.headline: Two ex-FBI officials charged with allegedly lying about Hunter Biden probe: DOJ

title: Brent crude oil tops $116, a six-month high, as tensions swell in the Middle East
description: watch nowBrent crude oil rose to a six-month high on Friday, as investors increasingly expect the U.S. to resume strikes on Iran in the coming weeks.
body: watch nowBrent crude oil rose to a six-month high on Friday, as investors increasingly expect the U.S. to resume strikes on Iran in the coming weeks. Brent futures gained 3.1% to close at $116.72 a barrel, the highest settlement for the international benchmark since April 29. U.S. West Texas Intermediate added 3.8% to settle at $103.27 a barrel.Iran's army chief, meanwhile, said the country's military is fully prepared for "asymmetric warfare" after strengthening its capabilities, according to the state media agency Tasnim. Brent added 6.2% for the week, the third consecutive week of gains. WTI advanced 2% for the week.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCrude oil futuresPresident Donald Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. was not negotiating with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon." His cryptic remarks came as U.S. officials told The New York Times that the U.S. and Israel have plans for fresh strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. Iran-allied Houthi militants have continued to strike Saudi Arabia.The U.S. State Department has ordered all non-essential personnel to leave Saudi Arabia due to the strikes. A drone attack targeting the Shaybah oil field Wednesday in the Eastern Region left two people dead and two injured, according to Saudi state media. At least two people were killed and eight injured in an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday.Oil giant Saudi Aramco have told staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely following a series of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Reuters reported.

schema.headline: Brent crude oil tops $116, a six-month high, as tensions swell in the Middle East

title: Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried
description: Travelers navigate security lines at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport Terminal 1 on March 23, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota.Stephen Maturen
body: Travelers navigate security lines at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport Terminal 1 on March 23, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota.Stephen Maturen | Getty ImagesFewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high and climbing, airline executives say that's just fine.The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares is more important than fully filling their planes or flying record numbers of travelers."We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making," American Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday. American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.Fares keep climbingThe price of plane tickets has skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects this holiday season to come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.The average Southwest Airlines fare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane. The airline's count of revenue passengers, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago, to about 33.5 million people.Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations. "Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.Since April — when airlines began warning in earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints compared with the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. While that's down less than 2% from last year, it follows years of growth.With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices going for $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have been focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible. Even despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that travel demand overall is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.And not every carrier is seeing a decline. United Airlines flew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than it did a year ago, and said its unit revenue rose by 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic."I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company's earnings call Wednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."Profit hitMost airlines are anticipating that fuel costs will continue to bite, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third.American, United, Delta Air Lines and Southwest all cut their profit forecasts for 2026 this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back on its goals for expanding capacity, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds. The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.Read more about airlines' race to win over big spendersAlaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel raceBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgradesUnited ditches more economy seats to make room for bigger premium cabins with new layoutsCaviar and privacy: Airlines' business-class wars are hereAmerican Airlines is arriving late to the luxury travel boom. Can it catch up?First-class seats are getting so fancy they’re holding up new airplanesAirlines can’t add high-end seats fast enough as travelers treat themselves to first classSmaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, including Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air, have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May. "Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.

schema.headline: Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried

title: Trump dropping some Canada tariffs but 'replacing' them with other products
description: The White House on Friday said it would drop tariffs on some Canadian goods, but replace them with other products from the major U.S. trade partner.Th
body: The White House on Friday said it would drop tariffs on some Canadian goods, but replace them with other products from the major U.S. trade partner.The move was revealed after Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, took credit for pushing the Trump administration to issue tariff exemptions on several categories of Canadian imports she says are "crucial" for her state's industries.But Collins' announcement, which The Wall Street Journal first reported, did not mention that while tariffs would be removed for some Canadian products, new ones would be added to the list of goods subject to steep U.S. duties. The White House announced the new tariffs less than an hour after Collins touted the new exemptions to the tariffs, which are unpopular in the state where she's fighting for reelection.President Donald Trump earlier Friday signed a proclamation "removing certain products" from the list of items that he slapped 50% tariffs on over the summer using a 96-year-old trade law.But he is "replacing those products with certain valves, carpets, waste products, and others," according to a White House fact sheet detailing the proclamation.The changes are being made to "further refine the scope of the tariffs on certain Canadian products," according to the fact sheet, which does not mention Maine.The new additions and removals from the list of goods covered by the "Section 338" tariffs will take effect Oct. 30, four days before the Nov. 3 U.S. election, the fact sheet said.Asked what Collins had agreed to in her conversations pushing Trump administration officials for lower tariffs on products affecting her state, her spokeswoman Phoebe Keller told CNBC that the senator "requested exemptions for products that are important to Maine and will continue to do so."Before the fact sheet was made public, Collins' office sent a press release crediting the senator with securing the new tariff exemptions on "nine categories of products crucial for Maine's agricultural industries."That announcement came as voters have already started casting ballots in the pivotal Maine Senate race, where Trump's unpopular tariffs have been a top issue.Collins' Democratic opponent, fifth-generation Maine logger Troy Jackson, quickly pushed back, insisting  Collins deserves blame for enabling Trump's tariff policies."Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire," Jackson said in a statement. Trump has slapped heavy tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods during his second term as president as he has escalated a trade war against the top U.S. economic partner. Many of those tariffs have put considerable strain on businesses in Maine, which imports far more products from Canada than from any other country.White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC in a statement Friday afternoon that Trump's latest tariff proclamation is part of his efforts to "address Canada's discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce.""The President is taking action in response to Canada's continued discrimination against and additional retaliation targeting U.S. commerce, with the goal of protecting American farmers, manufacturers, and workers," said Middleton. "This administration will continue to use every available tool to restore reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships and safeguard the economic prosperity and national security of the American people."Collins has previously touted her efforts to push back on the president's protectionist trade policies. In the first televised debate between Collins and Jackson on Oct. 6, the GOP incumbent took credit for removing some items from Trump's list of tariffs on Canadian goods, including road salt.Jackson fired back, "What about everything else? We can't eat road salt."In her press release Friday, Collins said she has asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "for tariff relief" for the Maine-centric products, stressing the "burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families.""I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally and largest trading partner," she said.According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Mexico is the largest U.S. trading partner.The products being exempted from the Section 338 tariffs include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and packing bags, refrigeration equipment, multiple forms of machinery and seaweed and algae products, according to Collins.

schema.headline: Trump dropping some Canada tariffs but 'replacing' them with other products

title: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
description: Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's
body: Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's being described as "Black October."Nearly 70% of all websites use PHP, according to some estimates. "In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year," John Milinovich, senior director of product management at Figma, wrote in a post on X on Thursday. "Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out."Researchers at Google's Wiz and the AI firm Calif discovered major vulnerabilities in PHP in August by using advanced AI models from OpenAI and Google. But by Tuesday, the warnings had spread online, prompting governments and businesses around the globe to scramble to contain the fallout. Major AI companies have been warning about the technology's advancing cybersecurity capabilities since April, when Anthropic announced a limited rollout of its powerful model called Mythos. Concerns mounted in July, when OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached a company called Hugging Face. Experts believe the PHP security flaws serve as the latest example of what's to come.Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, wrote in a post on X on Thursday that the cybersecurity landscape is likely to get "a lot worse" before it gets better."Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now," Clinton said. "Not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)"While many large companies have access to advanced models that they can use to harden their systems, serious bugs could be more challenging for small- and medium-sized businesses to address, Chris Krebs, former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told CNBC on Friday. He encouraged smaller companies to "constantly" scan for vulnerabilities, deploy patches as fast as possible or take legacy systems offline."This is a significant week or two in cybersecurity," Krebs told CNBC's "Squawk Box." "As I mentioned, 3% of all critical vulnerabilities ever discovered have been found in the last month."Figma's Milinovich encouraged individuals to set up two-factor authentication for "everything," use a password manager, set up an identity protection app and move smart devices to their own network. He added that people should lean in and experiment with AI to understand how powerful the tools have become. "While I still firmly believe that AI will be a net positive for humanity, it's more clear to me than ever that the societal and individual risk is very real, and is playing out NOW," Milinovich said.Krebs added that company leaders and employees should check in on their security teams."Make sure they're doing okay," he said. "They've had a heck of a week."—CNBC's Isabel O’Brien contributed to this reportWATCH: Chris Krebs on AI discovering cyber vulnerabilities: It’ll get worse before it gets better

title: Defense giant Saab sees orders triple after Gripen fighter jet deal with Ukraine
description: Swedish defense giant Saab reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year ear
body: Swedish defense giant Saab reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year earlier, boosted by a deal to supply Gripen fighter jets to Ukraine. New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor ($6.6 billion), up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier, beating FactSet expectations of 56.4 billion kronor.Third-quarter sales reached 20.6 billion kronor, ahead of FactSet expectations of 20 billion kronor. Earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) came in at 1.95 billion kronor, also beating forecasts of 1.9 billion kronor.Stockholm-listed shares closed 1.8% higher Friday, amid a mixed defense sector. The Stoxx 600 index ended the session down 0.3%.The results come as European governments race to turn defense spending pledges into military capability.Saab's order intake included a 24.6 billion kronor contract for 16 Gripen E fighter jets with the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration for Ukraine, signed in June and booked in the third quarter. Deliveries are scheduled for 2029-2030."The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said in a statement.Orders booked in the quarter also include a 10.1 billion kronor order for its military surveillance aircraft GlobalEye to an undisclosed customer in the Middle East, and an 8.7 billion kronor order to equip warships for the German Navy.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconEuropean defense stocks over the past 12 months. Saab, whose products range from Gripen fighter jets and submarines to missiles and advanced electronics, has seen exponential order growth since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.Even with an ever-growing order book, booming sales, and increasing profitability, Saab stock, like many of its peers, has taken a hit in recent months as some investors question whether valuations have run ahead of the industry's ability to deliver.Growing order bookRising geopolitical tensions, including recent airspace violations, drone incidents and ongoing conflicts, are driving demand for defense capabilities, Johansson said. He added that Saab is expanding production capacity and investments to help it meet growing customer needs."The long-term market outlook remains favourable," he said, as Saab reported that the order growth was driven by a more than sixfold surge in large orders to 52.1 billion kronor, while small orders rose 84% and medium-sized orders fell 16%.The total order backlog amounted to 364.2 billion at the end of September, up from 274.5 billion at the beginning of the year, marking a sixth consecutive quarter of order book growth.watch nowIn July, Saab said it was looking to boost its production of jets from 15 per year to between 20 and 30. "We can go further than that if we now get sort of partners involved in a more substantial way," Johansson told CNBC at the time. Johansson also emphasized that European governments must fundamentally rethink how they buy weapons, moving away from fragmented national procurement toward long-term partnerships with industry.More defense news‘Project Firepower’: Inside Rheinmetall’s gunpowder expansion as Europe races to replenish its ammunitionEurope’s defense boom faces a new test: Can it actually deliver weapons?Ukraine’s drone playbook is wreaking havoc in Russia — and upending where NATO wants to investTank maker KNDS postpones IPO amid market struggles for defenseDefense stocks plummet on reports Germany is scrapping warships; Rheinmetall stock down 18%Why Europe is suddenly betting big on drones

title: Musk's SpaceX is still restricting Starlink in Ukraine and the toll is rising
description: watch nowSpaceX's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a
body: watch nowSpaceX's Starlink internet system continues to be throttled in Ukraine as the stakes rise for the war-torn country, Ukrainian officials and a national security expert said Friday."Every day matters for Ukraine, because every Ukrainian life matters," wrote Denys Sienik, Ukraine's deputy ambassador to the U.S., in a Friday post on X."Our people are waiting for positive news, hoping that the restrictions will be lifted and our defenders will have the capabilities they need to protect lives," Sienik said. "Unfortunately, as of today, nothing has changed. We continue to wait."Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said.Despite recent comments from President Donald Trump that indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade. "They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited."Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in the Zaporizhzhia region take a camouflage case off a Starlink satellite communication terminal to be set up at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, October 16, 2026. Dmytro Smolienko | Future Publishing | Getty ImagesUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on.""Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are." Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel."While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google.Elon Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear. Democratic lawmakers have since called for an investigation into Musk and the Starshield throttling. A group of bipartisan lawmakers penned a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday urging the agency to "act expeditiously to expand its Starshield arrangements and ensure uninterrupted satellite communications support for Ukraine." The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump spoke to Musk by phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals. Trump said Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back."But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored. "I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him."Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service.Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors." On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed a letter of intent with Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release. "Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."-- CNBC's Eamon Javers and Lora Kolodny contributed reporting to this story.Read more CNBC tech newsMusk's clash with Ukraine accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives. title: Russia and Ukraine trade fresh strikes despite renewed push for U.S.-brokered peace talks
description: Russia and Ukraine continued trading intense strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure overnight, less than a day after the parties signalled that
body: Russia and Ukraine continued trading intense strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure overnight, less than a day after the parties signalled that peace negotiations were moving forward in U.S.-brokered talks.Russia unleashed a major attack on Ukraine's energy facilities, knocking out electricity for over 500,000 after strikes on energy facilities in the Zhytomyr, Volyn, Mykolaiv, Poltava, Khmelnytskyi and Rivne regions, Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Friday.Work has begun on emergency restoration where the security situation allows, the ministry added.DTEK, one of Ukraine's largest private energy companies, said an unspecified thermal power plant had stopped generating electricity after Russian shelling.Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in 2022, DTEK's thermal power plants have been attacked more than 230 times, the company said in a post on Telegram early Friday.watch nowMeanwhile, Russia's Ministry of Defense said that air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 443 Ukrainian drones overnight.The latest attacks come after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday for talks on how to end the conflict with Ukraine.Following the meeting, Putin told Russian television that Moscow was ready to resume U.S.-mediated talks with Kyiv in November."The ​goal of these talks will be to ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia after reaching ​peace agreements, in their final form, not as a result of a temporary ceasefire for some short period of time. We are ready to resume these contacts to achieve this goal," Putin said, Reuters reported.A so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Oct. 11 has failed to yield any meaningful outcome.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this week that Ukraine refrained from attacking Russian energy targets for three days but later resumed attacks, citing Russia's continued attacks on its infrastructure.Speaking to CNN late Thursday, Zelenskyy said he was ready for a ceasefire, but that Ukraine needed strong security guarantees.

schema.headline: Russia and Ukraine trade fresh strikes despite renewed push for U.S.-brokered peace talks

title: Doctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reaction
description: Dado Ruvic | ReutersLeaked confidential data. A major stock sell-off. Beneath the chaos surrounding Moderna and Merck's latest data on their personali
body: Dado Ruvic | ReutersLeaked confidential data. A major stock sell-off. Beneath the chaos surrounding Moderna and Merck's latest data on their personalized cancer vaccine, oncologists see something else: an important milestone in melanoma treatment.The companies on Thursday released detailed results from a phase 3 trial on their mRNA-based shot after partial data leaked on social media platforms earlier that day. The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% when given alongside Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda, compared with Keytruda alone. The combination also reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy, according to the trial on roughly 1,100 patients whose tumors were removed by surgery. The stock market's reaction contrasted with the assessment of six melanoma specialists, who told CNBC the results represent a clinically meaningful advance that could eventually become a standard of care for patients who undergo surgery first and have not received immunotherapy before their operation.watch now"This has the potential to be a major breakthrough in melanoma treatment and also cancer immunotherapy in general that will open the door to greater outcomes for patients," said Dr. Sekwon Jang, a melanoma specialist at Inova Schar Cancer and principal investigator at one of the trial's U.S. sites.Dr. Janice Mehnert, NYU Langone skin cancer specialist and trial investigator, added that "this is the first time we're seeing that when you add something to immunotherapy, you actually boost the efficacy of the immunotherapy." The vaccine is not far from potentially entering the market for the first time and reaching melanoma patients. In an interview ahead of the results, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the company is finishing a filing with regulators as it aims to get the drug fully approved next year. "It's a very, very happy moment for the field, for patients," he said. Major advance in melanomaAn immunotherapy like Keytruda wakes up the immune system to detect and attack cancer cells. Unlike preventative vaccines, which protect against infections that can cause cancer, Moderna and Merck's treatment acts like a blueprint to train the immune system to recognize and hunt residual cancer cells based on the specific mutations in an individual patient's tumor. The significance of the phase 3 data extends beyond delaying a recurrence, doctors said. Melanoma can become much more difficult to treat when it returns after surgery and spreads to distant parts of the body, such as the lungs, brain or liver. Patients with advanced disease may require additional treatments, including immunotherapy, radiation or further surgery, and those methods are not guaranteed to work.Preventing the cancer from returning could spare patients from ever facing the risks and complexities of metastatic disease altogether."If we can essentially cure more patients with earlier-stage melanoma and never have to deal with unresectable metastatic disease — that's a wonderful advance," said Dr. Michael Postow, chief of the Melanoma Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and an investigator on the trial. Ideally, patients in the future may be able to undergo surgery and receive the vaccine and Keytruda without needing further melanoma treatment, Postow told CNBC. Still, questions remain about whether the combination ultimately helps patients live longer, what the benefit looks like over longer periods of time and which patients benefit most. The results also leave open where the personalized vaccine would fit into a changing melanoma treatment landscape, some experts said.  The trial tested the vaccine after surgery, alongside Keytruda, rather than against immunotherapy regimens given before surgery. That's an approach increasingly used for eligible patients with resectable melanoma, where the primary tumor can be removed. The data does not show that using the vaccine approach is more or less effective than receiving immunotherapy before surgery.The medical community will get more clarity after Moderna and Merck present the detailed results at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference on Saturday. Investors diverged from doctorsModerna shares fell as much as 25% Thursday, before regaining some ground, after partial data from the trial leaked on social media. The sell-off came despite the positive results, underscoring the gap between the treatment's clinical promise and investor expectations for its commercial potential. Moderna shares are also up nearly 600% this year due to the cancer shot optimism, creating more potential for a Wall Street letdown.Investors had hoped the vaccine and Keytruda would replicate the results of an earlier phase 2 trial, which showed a roughly 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death at five years, RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh wrote in a note Thursday. Huynh described the phase 3 results as clinically meaningful and likely to support regulatory approval, but said the primary efficacy result landed at the low end of investor expectations.But there was a key difference in the studies: The phase 3 trial included patients with a broader range of risk profiles, including some at lower risk of recurrence than those enrolled in the earlier phase 2 trial, said Dr. George Ansstas, who leads the melanoma department at Washington University in St. Louis. That may have slightly tempered the results, since patients considered lower risk have less chance of recurrence to begin with."It's great data actually. It's overall consistent with what we've proven in the phase 2 trial," said Ansstas, who also worked on the phase 2 trial. The combination showed little difference from Keytruda alone during the first six months of treatment, the companies said. But a separate analysis of the phase 3 data offered a more encouraging signal about the treatment's effect after the six-month mark. The vaccine and Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 58% after that point, compared with Keytruda alone. The 42% figure comes from the primary analysis, which included patients' outcomes throughout the trial's follow-up period. The median follow-up was about two years at the time of the analysis, so the result reflects the overall treatment effect, not just what happened before or after the six-month mark.Ansstas said the benefit of the personalized cancer vaccine may take several months to emerge because each shot must be custom-manufactured, a process that can take roughly six weeks, while patients begin Keytruda in the meantime. After vaccination begins, the immune system also needs time and repeated doses to develop a response against tumors. That timeline could help explain why the group that received the combination regimen saw even greater benefits around six months, Ansstas said. Still, the explanation is a hypothesis rather than proof of when the vaccine's effect begins. Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD ​Anderson Cancer Center, also highlighted the relatively mild side effects associated with the vaccine, including injection-site reactions, as a positive. Keytruda and other cancer therapies can cause potentially serious immune-related side effects. Detailed safety results released on Saturday should help clarify the trade-offs of adding the vaccine to the immunotherapy regimen.More work to be doneFor Moderna, the stakes extend beyond melanoma. The company is working to build a business beyond its Covid vaccine, while Merck is preparing for the eventual loss of patent protection on Keytruda. The companies have several hurdles ahead of them, including selling an individualized therapy that takes several weeks to create for a patient at scale. "I think the downside is that it's super labor-intensive, and you're gonna have to make vaccines for each person, and so you can't just stockpile a million vaccines and then just ship it out when somebody needs it," said Dr. Adil Daud, professor of medicine and melanoma oncologist at the University of California San Francisco, who was the lead investigator on the phase 3 trial. "There is the time and expense, and it's probably going to cost like a lot of money."Moderna and Merck have not disclosed any details about the manufacturing costs for the vaccine. He added that most people who walk into the clinic with a tumor that has not been surgically removed may stick to receiving Keytruda before an operation because "that approach is simpler and doesn't put the patient through the delay" of creating the vaccine. Daud said he expects the vaccine combination to be used primarily in the adjuvant setting, after surgery, rather than replace established immunotherapy regimens given before an operation. For patients who receive immunotherapy before surgery but show little or no response, the vaccine combination could offer another option, he said, though that would likely be for a smaller group of patients.Moderna and Merck still need to validate the approach in other cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma. Success in melanoma does not automatically guarantee that the approach will work in other tumors."I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Merck Research Laboratories President Dean Li said in an interview ahead of the results. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."Moderna's Bancel sees a bright future for the vaccine, saying he believes it will eventually be able to help "literally thousands and then tens of thousands and then hundreds of thousands of people across different tumors around the world."

schema.headline: Doctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reaction
